I think this is mostly because of prohibition. Before prohibition there were thousands of distilleries, but after prohibition was passed into law only a handful were allowed to remain open for "medicinal purposes." Only one pre-prohibition distillery that remained open during prohibition is still around today (to my knowledge), and that is Buffalo Trace. All the other distilleries in America had to start from scratch when prohibition ended. Because whiskey in general and bourbon in particular takes so long to age, it has a huge initial investment cost and 3+ years before you see any revenue, let alone profits. This led to there being much fewer distilleries than there were pre-prohibition. I think there are a handful of "craft" distilleries that have opened up in the last decade (I can think of a few in Colorado, Texas, Oklahoma, and of course Kentucky), but it is still pretty cost-prohibitive to start a new whiskey company.

I suspect people would be surprised at how consolidated most industries actually are. Take the top 8 companies for a variety of industries and see what % market share they have - airlines, finance, consumer goods, computers, cosmetics.... Don't have time to follow up with research for now, but I think our corporate overlords deserve more credit than most people give them.
